title: A secret reached history
summary: Rotate first, then decide whether to rewrite history. What filter-repo does, what it costs, and why deleting the file is not enough.

steps.title: Deleting the file is not enough
body: You committed `appsettings.Production.json` with a real database password, and pushed. You delete the file and commit again. Is the secret gone?
B added the password  <- still in history; anyone can run: git show B:appsettings.Production.json
No. Every clone, fork, CI cache and backup has B. Automated scanners crawl public repos for keys within **minutes** of a push.

**So the first step is always: rotate the secret.** Revoke the key or change the password at its source, deploy the new one, and check the logs for misuse. Once rotated, the old value in history is worthless. Rewriting history is optional clean-up, never the fix.

steps.prompt: A live API key was pushed to a shared repo. Arrange the response in the right order.
lines: Revoke or rotate the key at the provider
Deploy the new key from a secret store, not from the repo
Check the provider's logs for use of the old key
Remove the key from the code and add the file to .gitignore
Optionally rewrite history and coordinate a force-push with the team
steps.explain: Containment first: a rotated key cannot be abused, whatever happens to history. Cleaning history is last, and only worth it for some cases.

steps.prompt: Why is rotating the secret more important than rewriting history?
options: The secret may already be copied (clones, forks, CI logs, scanners); only rotation makes those copies useless
Rotation also removes it from history
steps.explain: Treat any secret that reached a remote as compromised. History rewriting cannot reach other people's clones.

steps.title: Rewriting history to remove it
body: If you do clean history (for example the repo will become public), use **git filter-repo** (the recommended successor to `filter-branch`; BFG Repo-Cleaner is an alternative):
git filter-repo --path appsettings.Production.json --invert-paths   # drop the file from every commit
git filter-repo --replace-text secrets.txt                         # replace values listed in secrets.txt
- **Every commit from the first one containing the secret onward gets a new id** (their content or parents changed). Every open PR and every teammate's clone now holds the old history.
- Everyone must re-clone (or carefully reset) and old branches must not be pushed back, or the secret returns.
- The hosting platform may still cache old commits (PR refs, forks): ask their support to purge.

steps.prompt: A repo has 50 commits on `main`, numbered 1 (oldest) to 50. The secret was added in commit 31 and removed in commit 35. After `git filter-repo --replace-text`, how many commits on `main` have a new id?
steps.explain: Commits 31 to 34 change content; commits 35 to 50 do not contain the secret but their parents changed, so their ids change too. 50 - 31 + 1 = 20. Commits 1 to 30 keep their ids.

steps.prompt: Does this help once a secret was pushed?
items: Deleting the file in a new commit
Moving secrets into a vault or user-secrets
steps.explain: Prevention (secret stores, scanning, push protection) and rotation fix the problem. History edits alone leave every existing copy compromised.

steps.prompt: Match the tool to its job.
pairs: rewrite every commit to remove paths or text
keep development secrets out of the repo
the server rejects a push containing a known key pattern
read a file as it was in an old commit

steps.title: Model a history scrub
prompt: Model `filter-repo --replace-text` on one file's history. `contents[i]` is the file in commit `i` (oldest first). Write `Scrub(contents, secret)` returning:
- the new contents, with every occurrence of `secret` replaced by `***REMOVED***`;

- how many commits get a **new id**: every commit from the first that contains the secret through the last commit (later commits change because their parents changed). Zero if the secret never appears.
starter: static (List<string> Contents, int ChangedCommits) Scrub(List<string> contents, string secret)
solution: static (List<string> Contents, int ChangedCommits) Scrub(List<string> contents, string secret)
hints: `contents.FindIndex(c => c.Contains(secret))` finds the first affected commit.
template: Dojo.Eq("values replaced", new List<string> { "a", "pw=***REMOVED***", "pw=***REMOVED*** b", "b", "c" }, c1);
Dojo.Eq("every commit from the first leak changes id", 4, n1);
